text: What's New in OpenSim 4.5? By Ayman Habib Jul 17, 2024 Add a reaction OpenSim 4.5 is available for download from the OpenSim Simtk project page. https://simtk.org/frs/?group_id=91 We are pleased to announce the following new features, bug fixes, and other improvements in OpenSim 4.5. The new software includes improvements to the look and feel of the GUI, updated Conda packages to make it easier to use the OpenSim API through latest Python versions up to 3.11 and updated Docker containers ,

title: What's_New_in_OpenSim_4.5?_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: of the GUI, updated Conda packages to make it easier to use the OpenSim API through latest Python versions up to 3.11 and updated Docker containers , additional Moco functionality, and the introduction of FunctionBasedPath for function-based muscle wrapping leading to speed-ups in muscle-driven simulations using it . We also now distribute a version of the Rajagopal model with the OpenSim resources folder included in the OpenSim application. Release notes are provided below along with links to

title: What's_New_in_OpenSim_4.5?_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: of the Rajagopal model with the OpenSim resources folder included in the OpenSim application. Release notes are provided below along with links to full change logs for more detail. FunctionBasedPath for modeling muscle geometry: The new FunctionBasedPath is an alternative to GeometryPath that allows modeling muscle lengths and moment arms using multivariate polynomial functions. For models with many and/or complex wrapping surfaces, this could lead to improvements in computation time. We also

title: What's_New_in_OpenSim_4.5?_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: polynomial functions. For models with many and/or complex wrapping surfaces, this could lead to improvements in computation time. We also added PolynomialPathFitter , a utility class for converting the set of geometry-based paths (GeometryPaths) in an OpenSim model to a set of FunctionBasedPaths. We also provide a scripting example, examplePolynomialPathFitter, for Matlab and Python users which demonstrates how to use PolynomialPathFitter given a musculoskeletal model and reference motion. API

title: What's_New_in_OpenSim_4.5?_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: for Matlab and Python users which demonstrates how to use PolynomialPathFitter given a musculoskeletal model and reference motion. API Change Support for FunctionBasedPath necessitated the removal of the unnamed property ' GeometryPath' in PathActuator (and all derived classes including Muscle , PathSpring , Ligament , and Blankevoort1991Ligament ). Therefore, the property methods get_GeometryPath() , upd_GeometryPath() , etc., are no longer available and should be updated to the

title: What's_New_in_OpenSim_4.5?_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: ). Therefore, the property methods get_GeometryPath() , upd_GeometryPath() , etc., are no longer available and should be updated to the backwards-compatible methods getGeometryPath() and updGeometryPath() . Moco Functionality: OpenSim Moco is a software toolkit to solve optimal control problems with musculoskeletal models defined in OpenSim using direct collocation. In this release we made the following improvements: We updated the models in exampleMocoTrack and exampleMocoInverse to use

title: What's_New_in_OpenSim_4.5?_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: using direct collocation. In this release we made the following improvements: We updated the models in exampleMocoTrack and exampleMocoInverse to use FunctionBasedPaths, and made minor changes to improve the quality of the muscle activity solutions in these examples. All MocoGoals now have the methods setDivideByDisplacement() , setDivideByMass() , and setDivideByDuration() . These methods can be used to normalize the cost or endpoint constraint value in any MocoGoal by the model's total

title: What's_New_in_OpenSim_4.5?_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: , and setDivideByDuration() . These methods can be used to normalize the cost or endpoint constraint value in any MocoGoal by the model's total center-of-mass displacement, the model's total mass, and the total duration of the MocoProblem. (Experimental) We added new transcription schemes to MocoCasADiSolver based on state-of-the-art pseudospectral collocation methods. These schemes solve the dynamics of a model with high accuracy for relatively few collocation points, which help improve

title: What's_New_in_OpenSim_4.5?_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: collocation methods. These schemes solve the dynamics of a model with high accuracy for relatively few collocation points, which help improve convergence. These can be selected by passing "legendre-gauss-#" or "legendre-gauss-radau-#" to set_transcription_scheme() , where "#" is the number of collocation points in each mesh interval between 1 and 9. Note that these schemes currently cannot be used with models with kinematic constraints. Support for kinematic constraints with pseudospectral

title: What's_New_in_OpenSim_4.5?_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: and 9. Note that these schemes currently cannot be used with models with kinematic constraints. Support for kinematic constraints with pseudospectral collocation will come in the next API release. The utility function createExternalLoadsTableForGait() now outputs center of pressure locations for foot-ground contact force elements. Reference ground reaction forces can now be normalized when using MocoContactTrackingGoal , which may be useful for scaling tracking cost terms to similar magnitudes

title: What's_New_in_OpenSim_4.5?_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: reaction forces can now be normalized when using MocoContactTrackingGoal , which may be useful for scaling tracking cost terms to similar magnitudes as other (e.g., control effort) costs. This will be followed by a hands-on example on how to use the OpenSim C++

Activation dynamics A muscle can neither generate force nor relax instantaneously. The development of force is a complex sequence of events that begins with the firing of motor units and

title: Pulling_Out_the_Stops:_Designing_a_Muscle_for_a_Tug-of-War_Competition_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_Ope.json
text: generate force nor relax instantaneously. The development of force is a complex sequence of events that begins with the firing of motor units and culminates in the formation of actin–myosin cross-bridges within the myofibrils of the muscle. When the motor units of a muscle depolarize, action potentials are elicited in the fibers of the muscle and cause calcium ions to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The increase in calcium ion concentrations then initiates the cross-bridge

title: Pulling_Out_the_Stops:_Designing_a_Muscle_for_a_Tug-of-War_Competition_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_Ope.json
text: and cause calcium ions to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The increase in calcium ion concentrations then initiates the cross-bridge formation between the actin and myosin filaments. In isolated muscle twitch experiments, the delay between a motor unit action potential and the development of peak force has been observed to vary from as little as 5 milliseconds for fast ocular muscles to as much as 40 or 50 milliseconds for muscles comprised of higher percentages of slow-twitch

title: Pulling_Out_the_Stops:_Designing_a_Muscle_for_a_Tug-of-War_Competition_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_Ope.json
text: as little as 5 milliseconds for fast ocular muscles to as much as 40 or 50 milliseconds for muscles comprised of higher percentages of slow-twitch fibers. The relaxation of muscle depends on the re-uptake of calcium ions into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. This re-uptake is a slower process than the calcium ion release, so the time required for muscle force to fall can be considerably longer than the time for it to develop. The activation dynamics of muscle can be modeled with a first-order

In the model, activation is allowed to vary continuously between 0 (no contraction) and 1 (full contraction). In the body, the activation of a muscle is a function of the number of motor units recruited and the firing frequency of these motor units. Some models of excitation–contraction coupling distinguish these two control mechanisms (Hatze, 1976), but it is often not computationally

title: Pulling_Out_the_Stops:_Designing_a_Muscle_for_a_Tug-of-War_Competition_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_Ope.json
text: units. Some models of excitation–contraction coupling distinguish these two control mechanisms (Hatze, 1976), but it is often not computationally feasible to use such models when conducting complex dynamic simulations. In a simulation, the muscle excitation signal is assumed to represent the net effect of both motor neuron recruitment and firing frequency. Like muscle activation, the excitation signal is also allowed to vary continuously between 0 (no excitation) and 1 (full excitation). The

text: frequency. Like muscle activation, the excitation signal is also allowed to vary continuously between 0 (no excitation) and 1 (full excitation). The activation and deactivation time constants can be assumed to be 10 and 40 ms, respectively (Zajac, 1989; Winters, 1990). The primary difference between the activation model presented by Thelen and the one presented by Winters lies in their expressions for Loading , which differ only in the values of the two coefficients shown in parentheses in Eqs. 2 and 3: Loading

Equation 1 can be made to respect a lower bound on activation by first constraining both activation and excitation to remain between the minimum activation level (0.01 by default) and the maximum activation level (1.0 by default). Design Challenge The competition is a single-elimination tournament between pairs of

text: by default) and the maximum activation level (1.0 by default). Design Challenge The competition is a single-elimination tournament between pairs of muscles. Each match is a one-second forward dynamic simulation where each muscle starts with minimal activation (a = 0.01). The match is won by the muscle that has moved the block to its side of the arena at the end of the simulation. Your challenge is to specify the muscle–tendon parameters and excitation time history necessary to overcome the

text: Objective The force-producing properties of muscle are complex, highly nonlinear, and can have substantial effects on movement (see McMahon, 1984 for a review). For simplicity, lumped-parameter, dimensionless muscle models that are capable of representing a variety of muscles with different architectures are commonly used in the dynamic simulation of movement (Zajac, 1989). In this exercise, you will explore the differential equations that describe muscle activation and muscle–tendon

title: Pulling_Out_the_Stops:_Designing_a_Muscle_for_a_Tug-of-War_Competition_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_Ope.json
text: simulation of movement (Zajac, 1989). In this exercise, you will explore the differential equations that describe muscle activation and muscle–tendon contraction dynamics when using a Hill-type muscle model. You will use OpenSim to implement a simple muscle–tendon model and conduct simulations to investigate how various model parameters affect the dynamic response of the actuator. The lab will conclude with a Virtual Muscle Tug-of-War in which you will design an optimal muscle and compete

title: Pulling_Out_the_Stops:_Designing_a_Muscle_for_a_Tug-of-War_Competition_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_Ope.json
text: the dynamic response of the actuator. The lab will conclude with a Virtual Muscle Tug-of-War in which you will design an optimal muscle and compete against other user-generated muscles. May the best muscle win! By working through this lab, you will: Become familiar with the differential equations describing muscle activation and muscle–tendon contraction dynamics. Learn how to model and simulate muscle–tendon dynamics using OpenSim. Become comfortable with modifying existing code that models

title: Pulling_Out_the_Stops:_Designing_a_Muscle_for_a_Tug-of-War_Competition_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_Ope.json
text: dynamics. Learn how to model and simulate muscle–tendon dynamics using OpenSim. Become comfortable with modifying existing code that models muscle activation and muscle–tendon mechanics. Explore the effect of various model parameters and simulation conditions on the dynamic response of muscle. Design your own optimal muscle–tendon actuator to compete in a virtual muscle tug-of-war. text: using Eq. (2). Activation dynamics A muscle can neither generate force nor relax instantaneously. The development of force is a complex sequence of events that begins with the firing of motor units and culminates in the formation of actin–myosin cross-bridges within the myofibrils of the muscle. When the motor units of a muscle depolarize, action potentials are elicited in the fibers of the muscle and cause calcium ions to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The increase in calcium ion

text: are elicited in the fibers of the muscle and cause calcium ions to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The increase in calcium ion concentrations then initiates the cross-bridge formation between the actin and myosin filaments. In isolated muscle twitch experiments, the delay between a motor unit action potential and the development of peak force has been observed to vary from as little as 5 milliseconds for fast ocular muscles to as much as 40 or 50 milliseconds for muscles comprised

text: force has been observed to vary from as little as 5 milliseconds for fast ocular muscles to as much as 40 or 50 milliseconds for muscles comprised of higher percentages of slow-twitch fibers. The relaxation of muscle depends on the re-uptake of calcium ions into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. This re-uptake is a slower process than the calcium ion release, so the time required for muscle force to fall can be considerably longer than the time for it to develop. The activation dynamics of muscle can

In the body, the activation of a muscle is a function of the number of motor units recruited and the firing frequency of these motor units. Some models of excitation–contraction coupling distinguish these two control mechanisms (Hatze, 1976), but it is often not computationally feasible to use such models when conducting complex dynamic simulations. In a simulation, the muscle excitation signal is assumed to represent the net effect of both motor neuron recruitment and firing frequency. Like muscle activation, the excitation signal is also allowed to vary continuously between 0 (no excitation) and 1 (full

text: Darwin Xander Sahin Project Video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aKeD6dSGZos Project Files Download project files here: Compliant vs Rigid Tendon Project Files.zip Background Static optimization to minimize metabolic cost is a popular method for solving the muscle redundancy problem for locomotion and other common tasks. With any simulation, there is a balance to be made between model accuracy and computational efficiency. When performing static optimization, it is common to ignore tendon

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: there is a balance to be made between model accuracy and computational efficiency. When performing static optimization, it is common to ignore tendon elasticity, assuming a completely rigid tendon, in order to simplify the solver. When comparing two Hill-based musculotendon models, one with an elastic tendon and one with a rigid tendon, Mousavi et al. 2014 observed that rigid tendon models converged 7.3 to 9.5 times faster than compliant tendon models using the same implicit integrator. With

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: et al. 2014 observed that rigid tendon models converged 7.3 to 9.5 times faster than compliant tendon models using the same implicit integrator. With time savings of this magnitude, there is a clear place for rigid tendon modeling. On the other hand, we see from Kaneda et al. 2023 that some researchers found it worthwhile to model compliant tendon dynamics (even at the expense of removing the force-velocity effect) in order to accurately predict improvement of internal joint forces compared to

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: dynamics (even at the expense of removing the force-velocity effect) in order to accurately predict improvement of internal joint forces compared to instrumented knee data. We hope to explore how substantial the drop in accuracy is between the two models. Perhaps rigid tendon modeling is sufficiently accurate for muscles with a low ratio of tendon slack length to muscle optimum length. Our study will seek to learn more about the nuance of when it is best to model with compliant versus rigid

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: slack length to muscle optimum length. Our study will seek to learn more about the nuance of when it is best to model with compliant versus rigid tendons. Research Question(s) Can we implement tendon compliance into our static optimization algorithm? How do muscle activations and forces change for walking simulations when comparing rigid versus compliant tendon models? Methods Figure 1. High level pipeline for comparing rigid vs. compliant tendon models in static optimization. We used walking

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: tendon models? Methods Figure 1. High level pipeline for comparing rigid vs. compliant tendon models in static optimization. We used walking data from Dembia et. al 2017 as inputs to two different static optimization frameworks. One framework assumes a rigid tendon model, while the other assumes a compliant tendon model. We then compared the differences between the muscle activations and muscle passive forces to quantify the differences between rigid and compliant tendon models when used with

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: between the muscle activations and muscle passive forces to quantify the differences between rigid and compliant tendon models when used with static optimization. Model Selection The model used was a modified version of the one seen in Rajagopal 2016, a 3D musculo-skeletal model with 80 Hill-type muscle-tendon units activating the lower limbs and 37 degrees of freedom. However, in our modified version, we did not have any virtual torque actuators driving the upper body. The model was scaled

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: 37 degrees of freedom. However, in our modified version, we did not have any virtual torque actuators driving the upper body. The model was scaled based on 24 cadaver specimens and 21 young healthy individuals and the same model was used in both the rigid tendon and compliant tendon implementations. Static Optimization with Rigid Tendon Model The static optimization with rigid tendon framework is described in Figure 2. First, the scaled model is loaded (scaled_model.osim), then the inverse

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: The static optimization with rigid tendon framework is described in Figure 2. First, the scaled model is loaded (scaled_model.osim), then the inverse kinematics solutions are loaded (coordinates.mot), and finally inverse dynamics are solved after loading the ground reaction force files (grf.mot and grf.xml). After setting the model to ignore tendon compliance, the static optimization has all the necessary components to solve for muscle activations and muscle passive forces at each time point.

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: compliance, the static optimization has all the necessary components to solve for muscle activations and muscle passive forces at each time point. The algorithm then continues to loop through the static optimization for every timepoint until a full time-series plot is generated for all muscle activations and passive forces. Figure 2. Framework for static optimization with rigid tendon model. Static Optimization with Compliant Tendon Model When implementing the compliant tendon model into static

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: static optimization with rigid tendon model. Static Optimization with Compliant Tendon Model When implementing the compliant tendon model into static optimization, the first few steps were similar to implementing the rigid tendon model. The algorithm starts with loading a scaled model, loading solved kinematics, and then solving inverse dynamics. Next, the algorithm runs static optimization under the rigid tendon model for the first timestep. This is so there is an initial muscle activation

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: Next, the algorithm runs static optimization under the rigid tendon model for the first timestep. This is so there is an initial muscle activation value to use for future timesteps when equilibrating tendon and muscle forces. After the first time step, the algorithm sets the igore_tendon_compliance flag to false and solves a static equilibrium force equation between the tendon and muscle to solve for muscle length. After muscle length is determined, static optimization can be performed through

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: equation between the tendon and muscle to solve for muscle length. After muscle length is determined, static optimization can be performed through MATLAB’s fmincon function to solve for the current timesteps muscle activations and muscle passive forces. The algorithm then increments to the next time step and re-solves the equilibrate muscles equation using the newly solved activations, performs static optimization and continues to loop through the remaining timesteps until all muscle

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: equation using the newly solved activations, performs static optimization and continues to loop through the remaining timesteps until all muscle activations and passive forces are obtained. Figure 3. Framework for static optimization with a compliant tendon model. The equation for equilibrating tendon and muscle forces was adapted from Uhlrich et. al 2022 and is given as: Where F o m is the maximum force the muscle is able to exert. f T ( l m , l MTU ) represents the force multiplier of the

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: et. al 2022 and is given as: Where F o m is the maximum force the muscle is able to exert. f T ( l m , l MTU ) represents the force multiplier of the tendon and is a function of muscle length l m t k and muscle-tendon unit length l MTU ( t k ) . The force multiplier of the muscle can be expressed as the muscle activation of the previous timestep a( t k-1 ) multiplied by the muscle force-length multiplier f l l m and added to the muscle potential energy force multiplier f PE ( l m ) . Finally α(

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: t k-1 ) multiplied by the muscle force-length multiplier f l l m and added to the muscle potential energy force multiplier f PE ( l m ) . Finally α( l m ) represents the pennation angle of the muscle fiber. We have assumed muscle velocity to be zero and thus the muscle force-velocity multiplier f l ( v m ) to be 1 so we ignore it in our muscle force multiplier equation. The reason we assume muscle fiber velocity to be 0 is because if we had allowed muscle velocity to be an unknown variable, our

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: multiplier equation. The reason we assume muscle fiber velocity to be 0 is because if we had allowed muscle velocity to be an unknown variable, our equilibrate-muscle-force equation would become a differential equation with no guarantee of convergence when solving. Secondly, Ulhrich et. al 2022 show that this assumption of zero muscle velocity in compliant tendon models was comparable because it produced relatively accurate results similar to experimental EMG data. Muscle-tendon unit length for

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: tendon models was comparable because it produced relatively accurate results similar to experimental EMG data. Muscle-tendon unit length for the current timestep l MTU ( t k ) , muscle activation from the previous timestep are a( t k-1 ) , and maximum muscle force F o m are all known. The only unknowns in the equilibrate muscles equation are functions of muscle length of the current timestep l m (t k ) and thus the muscle length can be solved using a root-finding algorithm such as Newton’s

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: of muscle length of the current timestep l m (t k ) and thus the muscle length can be solved using a root-finding algorithm such as Newton’s method. Figure 6. RMSE vs Normalized Tendon Slack Length Ratio RMSE values were plotted against their normalized tendon slack length to determine why some muscles had high RMSE. text: Fit We performed a linear regression for which an r-squared constant of 0.15 suggests a weak positive correlation between normalized tendon slack length and RMSE in activation between rigid and compliant tendon models in static optimization. Figure 8. Filtered Percent Change in Passive Muscle Force vs Normalized Tendon Slack Length Ratio with Linear Fit Suspecting that muscle activations weren’t telling the whole story, we next investigated the correlation between normalized tendon length and

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: Fit Suspecting that muscle activations weren’t telling the whole story, we next investigated the correlation between normalized tendon length and the percent change in passive force between compliant and rigid tendon models. We computed percent change in passive force by taking the time series integral of passive force for rigid and tendon models, finding the difference, and then dividing by the time series integral for the rigid tendon passive force. Note that some muscles with excessively low

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: finding the difference, and then dividing by the time series integral for the rigid tendon passive force. Note that some muscles with excessively low passive force integrals were filtered from the data, as these had denominators approaching zero which yielded unreasonably high percent change in passive force. As you can see by all data points being below 0 on the y-axis, passive force exclusively decreases in the compliant tendon model for all muscles. Further, there is a stronger correlation

text: below 0 on the y-axis, passive force exclusively decreases in the compliant tendon model for all muscles. Further, there is a stronger correlation than we saw for activation of 0.66 between normalized tendon slack length and percent decrease in passive force. This is consistent with our expectation. Since the overall musculotendon unit length is determined by Inverse Kinematics, and is identical for both models, we expect to see that the muscle length change in rigid tendon models will be

text: is determined by Inverse Kinematics, and is identical for both models, we expect to see that the muscle length change in rigid tendon models will be greater to compensate for a rigid tendon, leading to higher passive forces. Figure 9. Total Muscle Force Error for Rigid Tendon Models (Millard 2013) Further, we see that our linear regression trend is supported by previous literature. Figure 9 shows a roughly linear trendline of total force error (comparing rigid and compliant tendon models)

text: is supported by previous literature. Figure 9 shows a roughly linear trendline of total force error (comparing rigid and compliant tendon models) versus normalized tendon slack length. Our regression line ends at roughly 60 percent error (signs are reversed) for normalized tendon length of 9, which is within the standard deviation bounds of Millard’s plot. Ultimately, if we reframe our results with consideration of our research question, we have found that modelling compliant versus rigid

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: plot. Ultimately, if we reframe our results with consideration of our research question, we have found that modelling compliant versus rigid tendon has some effect on muscle activation for most muscles, and slightly more so for muscles with a longer normalized tendon slack length. However, compliant tendon modelling has a significant effect (up to 60%) on the passive muscle forces and there is a strong correlation between the observed decrease in passive forces and the normalized tendon slack

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: 60%) on the passive muscle forces and there is a strong correlation between the observed decrease in passive forces and the normalized tendon slack length of the muscle. To distill these trends, we discovered that muscles with very low activation or force were often outliers and needed to be removed from linear regression computation. And finally, we have found previous literature such as MIllard et al. 2013 to support the trends in change of muscle force for compliant tendon modelling.

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: we have found previous literature such as MIllard et al. 2013 to support the trends in change of muscle force for compliant tendon modelling. Limitations One key limitation of our study is the assumption of zero muscle velocity when solving for static equilibrium between tendon and muscle forces in the compliant tendon model. While there have been preliminary studies that show that compliant tendon modeling with no force velocity multiplier matches experimental EMG data better than rigid tendon

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: preliminary studies that show that compliant tendon modeling with no force velocity multiplier matches experimental EMG data better than rigid tendon modeling with force velocity multiplier [7] it still is not a true direct comparison between rigid and compliant tendons. Another limitation is that we still had to use a rigid tendon model for the first timestep to initially solve for the first muscle activations in our compliant tendon model. This skews our results that are closer to the first

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: first timestep to initially solve for the first muscle activations in our compliant tendon model. This skews our results that are closer to the first few timesteps since the first muscle activation isn’t representative of what muscle with compliant tendon would feel. Future Work To learn more from our study, it would be informative to compare both models against EMG data collected for the same walking trials. This would allow us to make conclusions about how much better or worse compliant

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: both models against EMG data collected for the same walking trials. This would allow us to make conclusions about how much better or worse compliant tendon modeling successfully replicates real-world data compared to rigid tendon models. With our current analysis, we are only able to make statements about how the two are different, with no support for which model performs better. If compliant tendon modeling proves to be more accurate, the next point of comparison for consideration would be the

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: for which model performs better. If compliant tendon modeling proves to be more accurate, the next point of comparison for consideration would be the computation time for both models; this would allow users to consider the tradeoff of accuracy versus time spent. Next, it would be interesting to observe the effect of compliant tendon dynamics for different gaits or loaded walking to see how well the model performs in different activation patterns. And finally, for clinical application, it would

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: gaits or loaded walking to see how well the model performs in different activation patterns. And finally, for clinical application, it would be interesting to use the joint reaction analysis tool to compare against instrumented joint force measurements to evaluate how well the two models can predict improvement in internal joint forces for prescribing modified gait kinematics. text: of Rigid and Compliant Tendon Dynamics in Static Optimization for Gait Analysis By Carmichael Ong Jun 09, 2023 Add a reaction Team Members Brian Wu Ethan Darwin Xander Sahin Project Video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aKeD6dSGZos Project Files Download project files here: Compliant vs Rigid Tendon Project Files.zip Background Static optimization to minimize metabolic cost is a popular method for solving the muscle redundancy problem for locomotion and other common tasks. With any simulation,

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: to minimize metabolic cost is a popular method for solving the muscle redundancy problem for locomotion and other common tasks. With any simulation, there is a balance to be made between model accuracy and computational efficiency. When performing static optimization, it is common to ignore tendon elasticity, assuming a completely rigid tendon, in order to simplify the solver. When comparing two Hill-based musculotendon models, one with an elastic tendon and one with a rigid tendon, Mousavi et

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: order to simplify the solver. When comparing two Hill-based musculotendon models, one with an elastic tendon and one with a rigid tendon, Mousavi et al. 2014 observed that rigid tendon models converged 7.3 to 9.5 times faster than compliant tendon models using the same implicit integrator. With time savings of this magnitude, there is a clear place for rigid tendon modeling. On the other hand, we see from Kaneda et al. 2023 that some researchers found it worthwhile to model compliant tendon

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: for rigid tendon modeling. On the other hand, we see from Kaneda et al. 2023 that some researchers found it worthwhile to model compliant tendon dynamics (even at the expense of removing the force-velocity effect) in order to accurately predict improvement of internal joint forces compared to instrumented knee data. We hope to explore how substantial the drop in accuracy is between the two models. Perhaps rigid tendon modeling is sufficiently accurate for muscles with a low ratio of tendon

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: the drop in accuracy is between the two models. Perhaps rigid tendon modeling is sufficiently accurate for muscles with a low ratio of tendon slack length to muscle optimum length. Our study will seek to learn more about the nuance of when it is best to model with compliant versus rigid tendons. Research Question(s) Can we implement tendon compliance into our static optimization algorithm? How do muscle activations and forces change for walking simulations when comparing rigid versus compliant

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: into our static optimization algorithm? How do muscle activations and forces change for walking simulations when comparing rigid versus compliant tendon models? Methods Figure 1. High level pipeline for comparing rigid vs. compliant tendon models in static optimization. We used walking data from Dembia et. al 2017 as inputs to two different static optimization frameworks. One framework assumes a rigid tendon model, while the other assumes a compliant tendon model. We then compared the

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: static optimization frameworks. One framework assumes a rigid tendon model, while the other assumes a compliant tendon model. We then compared the differences between the muscle activations and muscle passive forces to quantify the differences between rigid and compliant tendon models when used with static optimization. Model Selection The model used was a modified version of the one seen in Rajagopal 2016, a 3D musculo-skeletal model with 80 Hill-type muscle-tendon units activating the lower

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: used was a modified version of the one seen in Rajagopal 2016, a 3D musculo-skeletal model with 80 Hill-type muscle-tendon units activating the lower limbs and 37 degrees of freedom. However, in our modified version, we did not have any virtual torque actuators driving the upper body. The model was scaled based on 24 cadaver specimens and 21 young healthy individuals and the same model was used in both the rigid tendon and compliant tendon implementations. Static Optimization with Rigid Tendon

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: healthy individuals and the same model was used in both the rigid tendon and compliant tendon implementations. Static Optimization with Rigid Tendon Model The static optimization with rigid tendon framework is described in Figure 2. First, the scaled model is loaded (scaled_model.osim), then the inverse kinematics solutions are loaded (coordinates.mot), and finally inverse dynamics are solved after loading the ground reaction force files (grf.mot and grf.xml). After setting the model to ignore

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: and finally inverse dynamics are solved after loading the ground reaction force files (grf.mot and grf.xml). After setting the model to ignore tendon compliance, the static optimization has all the necessary components to solve for muscle activations and muscle passive forces at each time point. The algorithm then continues to loop through the static optimization for every timepoint until a full time-series plot is generated for all muscle activations and passive forces. Figure 2. Framework for

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: optimization for every timepoint until a full time-series plot is generated for all muscle activations and passive forces. Figure 2. Framework for static optimization with rigid tendon model. Static Optimization with Compliant Tendon Model When implementing the compliant tendon model into static optimization, the first few steps were similar to implementing the rigid tendon model. The algorithm starts with loading a scaled model, loading solved kinematics, and then solving inverse dynamics.

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: implementing the rigid tendon model. The algorithm starts with loading a scaled model, loading solved kinematics, and then solving inverse dynamics. Next, the algorithm runs static optimization under the rigid tendon model for the first timestep. This is so there is an initial muscle activation value to use for future timesteps when equilibrating tendon and muscle forces. After the first time step, the algorithm sets the igore_tendon_compliance flag to false and solves a static equilibrium

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: tendon and muscle forces. After the first time step, the algorithm sets the igore_tendon_compliance flag to false and solves a static equilibrium force equation between the tendon and muscle to solve for muscle length. After muscle length is determined, static optimization can be performed through MATLAB’s fmincon function to solve for the current timesteps muscle activations and muscle passive forces. The algorithm then increments to the next time step and re-solves the equilibrate muscles

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: timesteps muscle activations and muscle passive forces. The algorithm then increments to the next time step and re-solves the equilibrate muscles equation using the newly solved activations, performs static optimization and continues to loop through the remaining timesteps until all muscle activations and passive forces are obtained. Figure 3. Framework for static optimization with a compliant tendon model. The equation for equilibrating tendon and muscle forces was adapted from Uhlrich et. al

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: for static optimization with a compliant tendon model. The equation for equilibrating tendon and muscle forces was adapted from Uhlrich et. al 2022 and is given as: Where F o m is the maximum force the muscle is able to exert. f T ( l m , l MTU ) represents the force multiplier of the tendon and is a function of muscle length l m t k and muscle-tendon unit length l MTU ( t k ) . The force multiplier of the muscle can be expressed as the muscle activation of the previous timestep a( t k-1 )

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: unit length l MTU ( t k ) . The force multiplier of the muscle can be expressed as the muscle activation of the previous timestep a( t k-1 ) multiplied by the muscle force-length multiplier f l l m and added to the muscle potential energy force multiplier f PE ( l m ) . Finally α( l m ) represents the pennation angle of the muscle fiber. We have assumed muscle velocity to be zero and thus the muscle force-velocity multiplier f l ( v m ) to be 1 so we ignore it in our muscle force multiplier

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: assumed muscle velocity to be zero and thus the muscle force-velocity multiplier f l ( v m ) to be 1 so we ignore it in our muscle force multiplier equation. The reason we assume muscle fiber velocity to be 0 is because if we had allowed muscle velocity to be an unknown variable, our equilibrate-muscle-force equation would become a differential equation with no guarantee of convergence when solving. Secondly, Ulhrich et. al 2022 show that this assumption of zero muscle velocity in compliant

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: equation with no guarantee of convergence when solving. Secondly, Ulhrich et. al 2022 show that this assumption of zero muscle velocity in compliant tendon models was comparable because it produced relatively accurate results similar to experimental EMG data. Muscle-tendon unit length for the current timestep l MTU ( t k ) , muscle activation from the previous timestep are a( t k-1 ) , and maximum muscle force F o m are all known. The only unknowns in the equilibrate muscles equation are

text: from the previous timestep are a( t k-1 ) , and maximum muscle force F o m are all known. The only unknowns in the equilibrate muscles equation are functions of muscle length of the current timestep l m (t k ) and thus the muscle length can be solved using a root-finding algorithm such as Newton’s method. Filtered Percent Change in Passive Muscle Force vs Normalized Tendon Slack Length Ratio with Linear Fit Suspecting that muscle activations weren’t telling the whole story, we next investigated the correlation between normalized tendon length and the percent change in passive force between compliant and rigid tendon models. We computed percent change in passive force by taking the time series integral of passive force for rigid

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: between compliant and rigid tendon models. We computed percent change in passive force by taking the time series integral of passive force for rigid and tendon models, finding the difference, and then dividing by the time series integral for the rigid tendon passive force. Note that some muscles with excessively low passive force integrals were filtered from the data, as these had denominators approaching zero which yielded unreasonably high percent change in passive force. As you can see by

text: filtered from the data, as these had denominators approaching zero which yielded unreasonably high percent change in passive force. As you can see by all data points being below 0 on the y-axis, passive force exclusively decreases in the compliant tendon model for all muscles. Further, there is a stronger correlation than we saw for activation of 0.66 between normalized tendon slack length and percent decrease in passive force. This is consistent with our expectation. Since the overall

Since the overall musculotendon unit length is determined by Inverse Kinematics, and is identical for both models, we expect to see that the muscle length change in rigid tendon models will be greater to compensate for a rigid tendon, leading to higher passive forces. Our regression line ends at roughly 60 percent error (signs are reversed) for normalized tendon length of 9, which is within the standard

text: length. Our regression line ends at roughly 60 percent error (signs are reversed) for normalized tendon length of 9, which is within the standard deviation bounds of Millard’s plot. Ultimately, if we reframe our results with consideration of our research question, we have found that modelling compliant versus rigid tendon has some effect on muscle activation for most muscles, and slightly more so for muscles with a longer normalized tendon slack length. However, compliant tendon modelling has a

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: activation for most muscles, and slightly more so for muscles with a longer normalized tendon slack length. However, compliant tendon modelling has a significant effect (up to 60%) on the passive muscle forces and there is a strong correlation between the observed decrease in passive forces and the normalized tendon slack length of the muscle. To distill these trends, we discovered that muscles with very low activation or force were often outliers and needed to be removed from linear regression

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: these trends, we discovered that muscles with very low activation or force were often outliers and needed to be removed from linear regression computation. And finally, we have found previous literature such as MIllard et al. 2013 to support the trends in change of muscle force for compliant tendon modelling. Limitations One key limitation of our study is the assumption of zero muscle velocity when solving for static equilibrium between tendon and muscle forces in the compliant tendon model.

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: study is the assumption of zero muscle velocity when solving for static equilibrium between tendon and muscle forces in the compliant tendon model. While there have been preliminary studies that show that compliant tendon modeling with no force velocity multiplier matches experimental EMG data better than rigid tendon modeling with force velocity multiplier [7] it still is not a true direct comparison between rigid and compliant tendons. Another limitation is that we still had to use a rigid

title: Comparison_of_Rigid_and_Compliant_Tendon_Dynamics_in_Static_Optimization_for_Gait_Analysis_-_OpenSim.json
text: multiplier [7] it still is not a true direct comparison between rigid and compliant tendons. Another limitation is that we still had to use a rigid tendon model for the first timestep to initially solve for the first muscle activations in our compliant tendon model. This skews our results that are closer to the first few timesteps since the first muscle activation isn’t representative of what muscle with compliant tendon would feel. This would allow us to make conclusions about how much better or worse compliant tendon modeling successfully replicates real-world data compared to rigid tendon models. With our current analysis, we are only able to make statements about how the two are

Inverse Kinematics Kinematics is the study of motion without considering the forces and moments that produce that motion. The purpose of inverse kinematics (IK) is to estimate the joint angles of a particular subject from experimental data. In this section, you will estimate a subject's joint angles during walking by performing an IK analysis using the subject scaled model and

text: data. In this section, you will estimate a subject's joint angles during walking by performing an IK analysis using the subject scaled model and experimentally collected walking data. For each time step of recorded motion data, IK computes a set of joint angles that put the model in a configuration that "best matches" the experimental kinematics. OpenSim determines this "best match" by solving a weighted least squares optimization problem with the goal of minimizing marker error. Marker error

Marker error is defined as the distance between an experimental marker and the corresponding model marker . Each marker has an associated weighting value, specifying how strongly that marker's error term should be minimized in the least squares problem. Objectives Purpose The purpose of this tutorial is to demonstrate how OpenSim solves an inverse kinematics and dynamics problem using experimental data. To diagnose movement disorders and study human movement, biomechanists frequently ask human subjects to perform movements in a motion capture laboratory and use computational tools to analyze these movements. A common step in analyzing a movement is to compute the joint angles and joint moments of the

title: Tutorial_3_-_Scaling,_Inverse_Kinematics,_and_Inverse_Dynamics_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: and use computational tools to analyze these movements. A common step in analyzing a movement is to compute the joint angles and joint moments of the subject during movement. OpenSim has tools for computing these quantities: Inverse kinematics is used to compute joint angles. Inverse dynamics is used to compute net joint reaction forces and net joint moments. Inverse kinematics computes the joint angles for a musculoskeletal model that best reproduce the motion of a subject. Inverse dynamics

title: Tutorial_3_-_Scaling,_Inverse_Kinematics,_and_Inverse_Dynamics_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: joint moments. Inverse kinematics computes the joint angles for a musculoskeletal model that best reproduce the motion of a subject. Inverse dynamics then use joint angles, angular velocities, and angular accelerations of the model, together with the experimental ground reaction forces and moments, to solve for the net reaction forces and net moments at each of the joints. Inverse Kinematics Kinematics is the study of motion without considering the forces and moments that produce that motion. The purpose of inverse kinematics (IK) is to estimate the joint angles of a particular subject from experimental data. In this section, you will estimate a subject's joint angles during walking by performing an IK analysis using the subject scaled model and experimentally collected walking

text: estimate a subject's joint angles during walking by performing an IK analysis using the subject scaled model and experimentally collected walking data. For each time step of recorded motion data, IK computes a set of joint angles that put the model in a configuration that "best matches" the experimental kinematics. OpenSim determines this "best match" by solving a weighted least squares optimization problem with the goal of minimizing marker error. Marker error is defined as the distance

title: Tutorial_3_-_Scaling,_Inverse_Kinematics,_and_Inverse_Dynamics_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: match" by solving a weighted least squares optimization problem with the goal of minimizing marker error. Marker error is defined as the distance between an experimental marker and the corresponding model marker . Each marker has an associated weighting value, specifying how strongly that marker's error term should be minimized in the least squares problem. For each time step, the inverse kinematics tool solves for a vector of generalized coordinates (e.g., joint angles), q , that minimizes the

The purpose of inverse dynamics is to

text: and moments that produce that motion. To perform inverse dynamics, estimation of mass and inertia is required. The purpose of inverse dynamics is to estimate the forces and moments that cause a particular motion, and its results can be used to infer how muscles are utilized in that motion. To determine these forces and moments, equations of motion for the system are solved iteratively [3]. The equations of motion are derived using the kinematic description and mass properties of a

Then, using the joint angles from inverse kinematics and experimental ground reaction force data, the net reaction forces and net moments at each of the joints are calculated such that the dynamic equilibrium conditions and boundary conditions are satisfied [3]. text: represented by S (including externally-applied forces as functions of time) poses unique challenges because these forces are not independent of the other forces acting on the model. In most cases, S represents the reaction forces due to the model's interaction with its environment. During walking, for example, the ground reaction force is the force applied to the model by the ground, which includes the contributions of gravity, velocity, and muscle forces to the reaction measured by a force

title: How_IAA_Works_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: applied to the model by the ground, which includes the contributions of gravity, velocity, and muscle forces to the reaction measured by a force plate. Since internal forces, such as muscles, do not directly accelerate the center of mass (it is the reaction force with the environment that causes the mass center acceleration), it is also necessary to determine how an internal force contributes to an external reaction force. Therefore, in computing the acceleration of the system due to individual

title: How_IAA_Works_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: determine how an internal force contributes to an external reaction force. Therefore, in computing the acceleration of the system due to individual force contributors, it is essential to decompose the external reaction force in order to include only the partial (induced) contribution of each internal force to the external reaction force and to the acceleration of the system. In this case, the acceleration induced by a single force contributor is: Loading where F i is the force contributor we

text: acceleration of the system. In this case, the acceleration induced by a single force contributor is: Loading where F i is the force contributor we are interested in analyzing, be it gravity, muscle forces, or ideal torque actuators. In this case, both the induced acceleration and the partial (induced) contact force, S i , are unknown. There are two fundamental approaches for solving this problem. One approach is to slightly augment (or perturb) the force of interest, F i , (by 1N) and integrate

title: How_IAA_Works_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: fundamental approaches for solving this problem. One approach is to slightly augment (or perturb) the force of interest, F i , (by 1N) and integrate the equations of motion a small interval forward in time to determine the corresponding change in the reaction force. This method is commonly referred to as a perturbation analysis . This approach yields the sensitivity of the contact force due to a unit change in force, and multiplying this change by the applied force yields its induced reaction

title: How_IAA_Works_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: the sensitivity of the contact force due to a unit change in force, and multiplying this change by the applied force yields its induced reaction force. There are several issues with this approach, including the need to use very stiff contact springs in order for the contact force sensitivity to remain linear over a small integration interval, which makes forward integration of the system dynamics slow. Second, results are sensitive to the selection of the contact stiffness and the time interval

title: How_IAA_Works_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: makes forward integration of the system dynamics slow. Second, results are sensitive to the selection of the contact stiffness and the time interval over which the change in contact force is evaluated. Applying stiff 3-dimensional linear and torsional springs approximates rigid constraints imposed by a weld constraint, effectively eliminating the 6 degrees of freedom at the point of contact. The other approach, which is the current implementation of the Induced Acceleration Analysis, replaces

title: How_IAA_Works_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: 6 degrees of freedom at the point of contact. The other approach, which is the current implementation of the Induced Acceleration Analysis, replaces the contribution of contact with an appropriate kinematic constraint. Kinematic constraint reaction forces are resolved simultaneously with the constrained equations of motion: Loading where the constraint matrix, C , maps from components of constraint reaction forces Loading , to a system generalized force (replacing the applied external force or

title: How_IAA_Works_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: matrix, C , maps from components of constraint reaction forces Loading , to a system generalized force (replacing the applied external force or compliant contact model, S ). The kinematic constraints on positions and velocities are differentiated so that they are expressed in terms of conditions on the coordinate accelerations. The left-hand side contains the accelerations and the right-hand side defines the conditions on accelerations described as a function, B , of time, system position,

title: How_IAA_Works_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: contains the accelerations and the right-hand side defines the conditions on accelerations described as a function, B , of time, system position, and/or system velocity. Using this approach with kinematic constraints does not require forward integration to estimate the response of contact as in the perturbation method, and results in a computationally efficient and precise analysis. title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: 3D marker coordinate data exported from a motion capture system will likely require some preparation before it is compatible with an OpenSim model. This page provides an overview of the different preparations that you may need to make before marker data is compatible with an OpenSim model. The process of preparing data has been made significantly easier by the tools developed by the OpenSim community. These tools simplify and automate much of the data preparation. These can be found in the

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: easier by the tools developed by the OpenSim community. These tools simplify and automate much of the data preparation. These can be found in the Tools for Preparing Motion Data page. OpenSim 4.0 OpenSim 4.0 includes new tools for preparing motion capture data that are not covered in this section. By looking in the CodeExamples folder in your OpenSim 4.0 files folder a Matlab script titled c3dExport.m is available. We recommend looking at this example script for more information on how to use

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: 4.0 files folder a Matlab script titled c3dExport.m is available. We recommend looking at this example script for more information on how to use OpenSim 4.0's new tools to make motion data preparation more convenient. Preparing File Format OpenSim only reads marker coordinate data formatted into .trc files. Marker coordinate files in other data formats, such as .c3d files, will need to be converted into .trc files before they can be used in OpenSim. This includes having a proper .trc header.

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: formats, such as .c3d files, will need to be converted into .trc files before they can be used in OpenSim. This includes having a proper .trc header. For more information on the .trc file format and how it is laid out see the Marker (.trc) Files page. Preparing Marker Names OpenSim associates digital markers attached to an OpenSim model to experimental marker data from .trc files by matching the experimental markers with model markers that have the same name. Because of this matching method,

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: marker data from .trc files by matching the experimental markers with model markers that have the same name. Because of this matching method, care must be taken to make sure that the marker names in the .trc file match the model marker names. Experimental marker names are taken directly from the column headings in the .trc file. Motion capture systems often give markers names like "Subject36_LASI" that have both a subject identifier and a marker location. These subject-specific names may not

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: often give markers names like "Subject36_LASI" that have both a subject identifier and a marker location. These subject-specific names may not match the names of the markers attached to the model. Model markers can be easily renamed within OpenSim to match the marker names in the .trc file. However, changing every model marker name manually in OpenSim for every subject becomes time consuming. To save time, renaming the .trc column headings to more general names such as "LASI" during data

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: in OpenSim for every subject becomes time consuming. To save time, renaming the .trc column headings to more general names such as "LASI" during data processing is recommended over changing model marker names. The process of changing the column headings in .trc files is generally easier to automate than renaming model marker names since the files containing experimental data are being edited anyway. Many tools exist for automated text-editing of tab-delimited files. Preparing the Marker

Preparing the Marker Coordinate System Motion capture systems may export data in a different coordinate system than the OpenSim model desired for analysis. If the lab coordinate system is rotated from the model coordinate system, then analysis will require a coordinate transformation beforehand. However, if the lab coordinate system is only translated from the model

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: system, then analysis will require a coordinate transformation beforehand. However, if the lab coordinate system is only translated from the model coordinate system then a coordinate transformation may not be necessary as long as external forces are applied in a way that agrees with the marker data. text: kayt.frisch@dordt.edu 3D marker coordinate data exported from a motion capture system will likely require some preparation before it is compatible with an OpenSim model. This page provides an overview of the different preparations that you may need to make before marker data is compatible with an OpenSim model. The process of preparing data has been made significantly easier by the tools developed by the OpenSim community. These tools simplify and automate much of the data preparation. These

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: been made significantly easier by the tools developed by the OpenSim community. These tools simplify and automate much of the data preparation. These can be found in the Tools for Preparing Motion Data page. OpenSim 4.0 OpenSim 4.0 includes new tools for preparing motion capture data that are not covered in this section. By looking in the CodeExamples folder in your OpenSim 4.0 files folder a Matlab script titled c3dExport.m is available. We recommend looking at this example script for more

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: folder in your OpenSim 4.0 files folder a Matlab script titled c3dExport.m is available. We recommend looking at this example script for more information on how to use OpenSim 4.0's new tools to make motion data preparation more convenient. Preparing File Format OpenSim only reads marker coordinate data formatted into .trc files. Marker coordinate files in other data formats, such as .c3d files, will need to be converted into .trc files before they can be used in OpenSim. This includes having a

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: files in other data formats, such as .c3d files, will need to be converted into .trc files before they can be used in OpenSim. This includes having a proper .trc header. For more information on the .trc file format and how it is laid out see the Marker (.trc) Files page. Preparing Marker Names OpenSim associates digital markers attached to an OpenSim model to experimental marker data from .trc files by matching the experimental markers with model markers that have the same name. Because of this

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: model to experimental marker data from .trc files by matching the experimental markers with model markers that have the same name. Because of this matching method, care must be taken to make sure that the marker names in the .trc file match the model marker names. Experimental marker names are taken directly from the column headings in the .trc file. Motion capture systems often give markers names like "Subject36_LASI" that have both a subject identifier and a marker location. These

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: the .trc file. Motion capture systems often give markers names like "Subject36_LASI" that have both a subject identifier and a marker location. These subject-specific names may not match the names of the markers attached to the model. Model markers can be easily renamed within OpenSim to match the marker names in the .trc file. However, changing every model marker name manually in OpenSim for every subject becomes time consuming. To save time, renaming the .trc column headings to more general

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: every model marker name manually in OpenSim for every subject becomes time consuming. To save time, renaming the .trc column headings to more general names such as "LASI" during data processing is recommended over changing model marker names. The process of changing the column headings in .trc files is generally easier to automate than renaming model marker names since the files containing experimental data are being edited anyway. Many tools exist for automated text-editing of tab-delimited

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: model marker names since the files containing experimental data are being edited anyway. Many tools exist for automated text-editing of tab-delimited files. Preparing the Marker Coordinate System Motion capture systems may export data in a different coordinate system than the OpenSim model desired for analysis. If the lab coordinate system is rotated from the model coordinate system, then analysis will require a coordinate transformation beforehand. However, if the lab coordinate system is only

title: Preparing_Marker_Coordinate_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: from the model coordinate system, then analysis will require a coordinate transformation beforehand. However, if the lab coordinate system is only translated from the model coordinate system then a coordinate transformation may not be necessary as long as external forces are applied in a way that agrees with the marker data. Details on how to reconcile coordinate systems are given in the Coordinate Systems in OpenSim page. Next: Preparing Force Data Previous: Preparing a Model for Analysis

text: Recent developments in the design of soft exosuits have been shown to effectively assist human locomotion. A variety of joint configurations (ankle + hip, Quinlivan et al 2017; hip, Ding et al 2016; etc) and assistive strategies have reduced the metabolic cost of walking by 5 to 20 percent. However, the human-device interaction across the design space has yet to be fully characterized, given time and cost limitations in the laboratory setting. Computational modeling and simulation approaches

text: demo video Draft final report Methods Our general optimization approach was solving a muscle redundancy problem using the Gait2354 OpenSim default model and associated data. The problem formulation is based on the direct collocation optimal control framework for solving the muscle redundancy published by Friedl De Groote. A cost function was minimized subject to a set of constraints including tracking the joint moments calculated from inverse dynamics. The joint moments are made up of

title: Simulation-based_soft_exosuit_design_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: was minimized subject to a set of constraints including tracking the joint moments calculated from inverse dynamics. The joint moments are made up of contributions from the muscles, reserve actuators, and assistive moments from the exosuit. Depending on the problem being solved, the assistive torques of the device were either prescribed or solved for as part of the optimization. We wanted to see if we could recreate their metabolic cost savings and predict what would happen above the maximum condition they tested. Exosuit Joint Tradeoff The next question we investigated is if we are given a single actuator, how should we allocate assistive moments across the exosuit to cause the greatest reduction in metabolic cost? We introduced a tradeoff parameter, alpha, to allow us to weight the assistance between multiple joints. Hip and Ankle The first

Hip and Ankle The first case we investigated is similar to the Quinlivan study in that we only assist at the ankle and hip. In this case, positive values of alpha means the hip flexion moment would be assisted more than the ankle plantar-flexion moment and vice-versa for negative values of alpha. In this problem we are optimizing for alpha and the exosuit activation over a

We found that instead of getting a bowl shaped curve for change in metabolic rate, the values plateau at larger peak assistive forces. This can be seen in the exosuit moment plots because all of the curves collapse on top of each other at the higher forces. Interestingly, we find that the optimized assistive hip

text: using the Gait2354 OpenSim default model and associated data. The problem formulation is based on the direct collocation optimal control framework for solving the muscle redundancy published by Friedl De Groote. A cost function was minimized subject to a set of constraints including tracking the joint moments calculated from inverse dynamics. The joint moments are made up of contributions from the muscles, reserve actuators, and assistive moments from the exosuit. Depending on the problem being

Depending on the problem being solved, the assistive torques of the device were either prescribed or solved for as part of the optimization. Quinlivan 2017 In this first problem, the goal was to simulate the experiments done with the soft exosuit in a paper by Quinlivan et al. We wanted to see if we could recreate their metabolic cost savings and predict what would happen above the

title: Simulation-based_soft_exosuit_design_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: exosuit in a paper by Quinlivan et al. We wanted to see if we could recreate their metabolic cost savings and predict what would happen above the maximum condition they tested. The cost function for this problem was a sum of excitations and activations of the muscles used to create the desired walking motion. For the first four conditions (blue curves), the exosuit moments were pulled directly from the paper. The next six conditions are scaled versions of these curves. The applied moments are

The simulation results are shown as colored dots and the experimental results from the paper are shown as bars. The simulations results however, underestimate the metabolic savings at the higher force levels. All metabolic costs were calculated using the Umberger metabolics model. text: model. The simulations suggest that there is some opportunity to further decrease metabolic cost with with device by increasing the assistive force above the maximum experimental trial, but the linear trend seen in the paper doesn't continue indefinitely. A bowl shape curve was found for metabolic savings over the 10 force levels tested. The initial decrease in metabolic cost can be seen because of muscles such as the medial gastrocnemius and illiacus which are assisted by the device. Their

Other muscles however, such as the tibialis anterior, are fighting against the device so their activation goes up with assistance level increasing metabolic cost. text: increasing metabolic cost. Exosuit Joint Tradeoff The next question we investigated is if we are given a single actuator, how should we allocate assistive moments across the exosuit to cause the greatest reduction in metabolic cost? We introduced a tradeoff parameter, alpha, to allow us to weight the assistance between multiple joints. title: Simulation-based_soft_exosuit_design_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: Ankle The first case we investigated is similar to the Quinlivan study in that we only assist at the ankle and hip. In this case, positive values of alpha means the hip flexion moment would be assisted more than the ankle plantar-flexion moment and vice-versa for negative values of alpha. In this problem we are optimizing for alpha and the exosuit activation over a range of maximum actuator forces. We found that instead of getting a bowl shaped curve for change in metabolic rate, the values

text: activation over a range of maximum actuator forces. We found that instead of getting a bowl shaped curve for change in metabolic rate, the values plateau at larger peak assistive forces. This can be seen in the exosuit moment plots because all of the curves collapse on top of each other at the higher forces. text: assistive hip moment exceeds the inverse dynamics moment. This means there were more benefits to assisting the ankle with this profile than there were costs associated with exceeding the hip moment . Hip, Knee and Ankle The next case we explored included adding an assistive moment at the knee. In the current device, the load path passes through the knee center. If we shifted the moment arm of the device at the hip to assist in more hip flexion the load path would pass in front of the knee center and we would assist in knee extension. title: Preparing_Force_Data_-_OpenSim_Documentation_-_OpenSim.json
text: an accurate dynamic simulation, external force data must be correctly prepared. One of the most common sources of external force data is a force plate. text: do not increase the maximum isometric force excessively unless you know its consequences in the muscle model. The Show Axes option is a toggle. A check next to it indicates that the coordinate axes are already being displayed. In this case, clicking on the option will turn off the coordinate axes display. If the axes are not being displayed and the Show Axes option is clicked, then the axes will appear. For joint nodes, there are two similar options: Toggle Child Frame and Toggle Parent Frame . As with the Show Axes option for a body node, the Toggle Child Frame and the Toggle Parent Frame options are toggle buttons, as their names indicate, accessible via the right mouse button. You

text: two halves) We now connect the bodies, and thus define how they can move with respect to one another. The cat is free to move about in space, and we represent this using a 6-degree-of-freedom joint between the ground (the inertial frame) and the cat's anterior body. We could use a FreeJoint, which is simpler to define, but we instead employ a CustomJoint. In our case, we do so because we want to specify the type of Euler angles that describe the orientation of the cat's anterior segment.

text: a CustomJoint. In our case, we do so because we want to specify the type of Euler angles that describe the orientation of the cat's anterior segment. Although the FreeJoint also uses Euler angles, it does not allow the modeler to choose which type of Euler angles are used. We choose YZX Euler angles, named yaw , pitch , and roll respectively, to avoid representation singularities. We specify this via a SpatialTransform object, which we'll use to define our CustomJoint.
